strengths: Addresses an important problem: preserving detailed video information while reducing long-context attention costs. Applying sparse attention to vision tokens while retaining dense attention for text is a sensible design.
Evaluates six benchmarks spanning long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial understanding, including a dense model fine-tuned on the same dataset.

Table 1 reports promising temporal-reasoning gains: Tomato improves from 22.6 to 26.5 over the base model. Studies of frame–resolution allocation, branch combinations, and gating provide useful empirical observations.
weaknesses: The central efficiency claim is inadequately supported. The reported 3.6% attention budget counts selected blocks and sliding-window attention but omits compressed-key attention and dense text attention. Attending from L queries to approximately L/s compressed keys costs O(L²/s) at fixed block size, contradicting the stated linear compression-branch complexity. Figure 6 provides branch timings without dense or competing-method comparisons; end-to-end latency, peak memory, and training-speed comparisons are missing.

Novelty beyond NSA is limited: compression, selection, sliding windows, and learned gating are inherited components. The principal adaptations are modality-specific attention and frame-level averaging. There are no controlled comparisons against straightforward NSA adaptation, alternative compression operators, or fixed gating that establish the value of these particular design choices.

The branch ablations do not specify whether reduced-branch models were retrained or branches were disabled only during inference. Removing branches from a jointly trained model can cause distribution and output-scale shifts, so the large accuracy drops do not establish that all three branches or dynamic gating are necessary.

Reliable improvement with longer context is overstated. Table 18 shows LongTimeScope falling from 44.4 at 512 frames × 128 tokens to 38.7 at 512 × 256; Table 21 shows MLVU falling from 51.8 to 48.6 for the same increase. These results demonstrate task-dependent context sensitivity rather than consistently beneficial scaling to 128K.

Reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence in the comparisons. VideoNSA scores differ between Tables 1 and 3 without clearly identified configuration changes. VisionZip and VScan scores are reversed between Table 1 and Tables 6 and 10. Several spatial baseline scores also differ between Tables 1 and 11. Table 27, labeled MLVU, reproduces Tomato results.

The evaluation does not establish a fair accuracy–efficiency frontier: compression baselines use their original sampling and retention settings, while sparse baselines use settings matched to VideoNSA. Actual compute budgets and method-specific tuning are not documented sufficiently. Improvements over strong sparse baselines are often small, LongTimeScope ties MInference, and spatial accuracy is below the strongest baseline; uncertainty estimates are absent.

The attention-sink analysis supports descriptive observations more than causal conclusions. Averaging, branch-specific normalization, and unnormalized sigmoid gating complicate comparisons of attention scores and value norms. No controlled intervention establishes that reducing measured sinks causes the accuracy gains.

strengths: The problem is relevant: preserving detailed video information while reducing long-context attention costs. Applying sparse attention to vision tokens while retaining dense attention for text is a reasonable design.

Evaluation spans six benchmarks covering long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial understanding, with several compression and sparse-attention baselines and a dense model fine-tuned on the same dataset.

The reported results show promise, particularly on Tomato (26.5 versus 22.6 for the backbone) and VSIBench (36.1 versus 29.7). The context-allocation sweeps and sparse-to-dense weight-transfer experiment provide useful exploratory evidence.
weaknesses: The central efficiency claim is inadequately supported. The 3.6% attention-budget calculation counts selected blocks and sliding-window attention but omits attention to compressed tokens and dense text attention. With fixed compression block size, attending from L queries to approximately L/s compressed tokens still costs O(L²/s), contradicting the claimed approximately linear compression complexity. Figure 6 reports only internal branch latencies; there are no comparative end-to-end latency, throughput, peak-memory, or training-efficiency measurements establishing an advantage over FlashAttention and competing methods.

The methodological novelty is limited and insufficiently isolated. Compression, block selection, sliding-window attention, and learned branch gates are inherited from NSA. The principal adaptations are modality-specific attention and frame-based averaging. There is no controlled comparison with a straightforward NSA adaptation, alternative block construction, or sparse attention applied to both modalities to establish the value of these particular choices.

Comparative gains are less conclusive than the claims suggest. In Table 1, VideoNSA exceeds the strongest listed sparse baseline by only 0.5 points on LongVideoBench and 0.6 on TimeScope, ties MInference on LongTimeScope, and trails the best sparse baseline on VSIBench. No uncertainty estimates are provided. Baselines use heterogeneous sampling/compression settings, and no matched-cost accuracy comparison is reported. The selection protocol for benchmark-specific attention and input configurations is also unclear.

The branch ablations do not establish that all three branches or dynamic gating are necessary. The manuscript does not explain whether reduced-branch models were independently retrained or merely modified at inference. Removing branches from a jointly trained model introduces distribution and output-scale changes. Independently trained, budget-matched variants and fixed-gate controls are needed to support the architectural conclusions.

Results and configurations contain substantial unresolved inconsistencies. LongVideoBench accuracy is 60.0 in Table 1, 59.4 in Table 3, and 60.2 in Table 7 without a clear mapping to configurations. VisionZip and VScan exchange LongTimeScope scores between Tables 1 and 6; several VSIBench baseline scores also differ between Tables 1 and 11. Table 27 is labeled MLVU but reproduces Tomato-style results. These discrepancies prevent reliable interpretation of rankings and reproduction of the headline results.

The scaling conclusion is overstated. Executing at 128K tokens demonstrates feasibility, but performance does not consistently improve with longer context: LongTimeScope and MLVU peak around 64K and decline at several 128K configurations. Corresponding dense and competing sparse-method scaling curves are missing, so the experiments do not isolate an extrapolation advantage attributable to VideoNSA.

The attention-sink analysis is descriptive rather than causal. Branches have different supports, normalization, and value distributions, making sink-rate comparisons dependent on aggregation details that are not adequately specified. No intervention establishes that learned gating reduces harmful sinks or that sink reduction improves task performance. Reproducibility is further limited by missing selection-score and masking details and blank code/model links.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: extending video-language models to long contexts while retaining fine-grained visual information. Applying sparse attention to vision tokens while preserving dense attention for text is a sensible design.

Evaluates six benchmarks spanning long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial understanding, including several compression and sparse-attention baselines and a dense model fine-tuned on the same dataset.

Reports promising accuracy, particularly on Tomato: 26.5 versus 22.6 for the original backbone and 23.7 for the strongest listed sparse baseline. The context-allocation experiments and branch analyses provide useful empirical observations.
weaknesses: The central efficiency claim is inadequately supported. Figure 6 reports only VideoNSA branch latency, without comparative end-to-end latency, throughput, peak memory, or training efficiency against dense and sparse baselines. Consequently, the practical benefit of the hardware-aware design remains unestablished.

The attention-budget calculation excludes the compression branch and dense text attention, so the advertised 3.6% is not the complete attention cost. Moreover, attending from L queries to approximately L/s compressed blocks costs O(L²/s) for fixed block size s; describing the compression branch as approximately linear and claiming near-linear overall scalability requires correction or stronger qualification.

Novelty beyond the original NSA is limited: compression, block selection, sliding windows, and learned gates are inherited. The principal adaptations are modality-specific routing and frame-oriented averaging, but there are no controlled comparisons isolating these choices against a straightforward NSA adaptation, fixed gating, or alternative block layouts.

Reported results contain material inconsistencies. VideoNSA's LongVideoBench score is 60.0 in Table 1, 59.4 in Table 3, and 60.2 in Table 7. VisionZip and VScan scores are exchanged between the main table and the detailed LongTimeScope and Tomato tables, and several VSIBench baseline values also disagree. Table 27 is labeled MLVU but contains Tomato categories and results. These discrepancies prevent reliable interpretation of the comparisons.

The evaluation does not clearly distinguish configuration selection from final testing. Extensive benchmark-specific frame, resolution, and attention-budget sweeps are reported without an explicit held-out selection protocol or equally documented tuning for competitors. Several gains over strong baselines are small, LongTimeScope ties MInference, and VSIBench trails the strongest sparse methods; no uncertainty estimates establish the robustness of these differences.

The ablations do not establish whether branch subsets were separately trained or merely disabled during inference. Without matched retraining and a fixed-gate control, their degradation cannot establish the necessity of the proposed architecture or dynamic gating. Likewise, attention-sink visualizations do not demonstrate that reducing sinks causes improved performance.

Scaling claims exceed the evidence: successful inference at 128K is demonstrated, but accuracy does not consistently improve with context length. LongTimeScope and MLVU peak around 64K and decline under several 128K configurations. Reproducibility is also limited by missing exact baseline configurations, unclear masking and handling of interleaved text/video tokens, and absent accessible code or model links.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: preserving fine-grained video information while reducing long-context attention costs. Using sparse attention for visual tokens and dense attention for text is a sensible adaptation.

Evaluates eight benchmarks spanning long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial reasoning, with multiple compression and sparse-attention baselines and a dense baseline fine-tuned on the same data.
Reports useful empirical gains, particularly on Tomato and LSDBench, and demonstrates inference up to 128K tokens after training at 36K.

Includes substantial diagnostic experiments on context allocation, attention budgets, branch removal, dynamic versus static gates, and kernel overhead. Appendix Q reports a modest training-cost reduction from 5280 to 4600 H100 GPU-hours.
weaknesses: The methodological contribution is limited relative to existing NSA: the three branches and learned gating are inherited, while the principal adaptations are modality-specific attention and frame-level averaging. Experiments do not isolate the value of these adaptations against a straightforward NSA transfer, alternative pooling, or sparse attention applied to both modalities.

The headline 3.6% attention-budget claim omits the compression branch and dense text attention. The compression branch attends from visual queries to compressed blocks, retaining an O(L²/s) term for fixed block size s. Consequently, the stated budget is not the total attention cost, and claims of near-linear scalability are not established. Section 4 also incorrectly describes the compression branch as ideally linear.

Practical acceleration over an optimized dense baseline is unconvincing. Figure 26 reports approximately 3.1× speedup for both VideoNSA and Flash Attention at 128K relative to 'Full Attention'; VideoNSA is slower than Flash Attention at shorter contexts and slower than several sparse baselines at 128K. Table 35 reports practical FLOPs of 0.56× dense, substantially above the ideal estimate. End-to-end latency and peak-memory measurements are missing despite the efficiency and memory claims.

Several accuracy improvements over strong sparse baselines are small or absent: VideoNSA ties MInference on LongTimeScope and trails XAttention on VSIBench. No uncertainty estimates are provided. Baselines use differing sampling and retention settings, and the paper does not establish accuracy–latency tradeoffs under matched budgets or clearly separate benchmark tuning from final evaluation.

The ablations support dependence on the trained architecture more clearly than architectural necessity. It is unclear whether branch-removal variants were retrained, and replacing learned gates with averages at inference introduces distribution shift. These interventions do not establish that three branches or dynamic gating outperform properly trained alternatives. Likewise, attention-sink visualizations do not demonstrate that reducing sinks causes the accuracy gains.

Reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence and reproducibility. Tables 1 and 3 give different VideoNSA scores without explanation; Table 31, labeled MLVU, repeats Tomato-style results; and Table 5 reverses the apparent units for Tomato's frame and token settings. The treatment of frame-aligned blocks when evaluation resolution changes is unclear, and the project, code, and model links are blank. These issues compound the unresolved efficiency accounting and limited novelty, leaving the submission below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The problem is relevant: retaining detailed video evidence while reducing long-context attention costs. Frame-aligned sparse attention with dense text attention is a sensible adaptation of NSA to video-language models.

Evaluation covers long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial understanding, with additional benchmarks in the appendix. Comparisons include multiple sparse and compression baselines and a dense model fine-tuned on the same dataset.

There are meaningful positive results, particularly on Tomato (26.5 versus 23.7 for the strongest listed sparse baseline) and LSDBench (55.2 versus 52.3). Context-allocation experiments and the static-gate ablation provide useful empirical insights.

The appendix supplies training hyperparameters, detailed benchmark results, and actual efficiency measurements, including candid discussion of kernel padding overhead and a roughly 13% reduction in training GPU-hours.
weaknesses: The methodological contribution beyond existing NSA is limited and insufficiently isolated. Compression, selection, sliding-window attention, and learned branch gates are inherited; the main adaptations are frame-aligned averaging and modality-specific attention. There is no controlled comparison against straightforward NSA adaptation or ablations isolating frame alignment and dense text attention.

The efficiency evidence does not establish a practical advantage over optimized dense attention. In Figure 26, VideoNSA is slower than Flash Attention through 64K and approximately matches it at 128K; several sparse baselines are faster. Reporting 3.1× speedup over the separate 'Full Attention' implementation obscures this distinction. Table 35 also reports substantially higher FLOPs than XAttention. Accuracy–latency trade-offs and peak-memory measurements are needed to substantiate the central efficiency claims.

The attention-budget and scaling arguments are technically incomplete. The advertised 3.6% budget counts selected blocks and sliding-window attention but excludes compressed-branch attention and dense text attention. Attending from L queries to approximately L/s compressed blocks costs O(L²/s) at fixed block size, contradicting the assertion that the compression branch ideally scales linearly and weakening the conclusion's near-linear scalability claim.

Most main-table gains over strong sparse baselines are modest: 0.5 points on LongVideoBench and 0.6 on TimeScope, with a tie on LongTimeScope and lower VSIBench accuracy than XAttention and MInference. No uncertainty estimates establish the reliability of small improvements. The dense fine-tuning control is useful, but comparisons against exclusively training-free sparse baselines do not isolate the benefit of the proposed adaptations from additional training.

Important experimental details remain ambiguous. The branch-removal study does not clearly state whether reduced models were independently trained or branches were disabled at inference; the latter would not establish architectural necessity. Benchmark-specific allocation tuning lacks a clearly documented held-out selection protocol. Section 2.2 also ties block size to frame token count, whereas later experiments fix block size at 64 while varying frame resolution.

Results are inconsistent across tables without explanation. VideoNSA's LongVideoBench score is 60.0 in Table 1, 59.4 in Table 3, and 60.2 in Table 7; TimeScope and Tomato also change between Tables 1 and 3. VisionZip and VScan's LongTimeScope scores are exchanged between Tables 1 and 6. These discrepancies impede verification of the reported comparisons.

Mechanistic conclusions exceed the evidence. Gate weights and attention-sink distributions are descriptive and do not establish that sink suppression causes improved reasoning. Appendix M assumes routing stability under denser sampling rather than demonstrating it. Overall, the promising application and extensive experiments do not resolve the novelty, technical-accounting, and evaluation issues sufficiently for acceptance.

strengths: The hybrid design is sensible: sparse attention processes video tokens while dense attention preserves text access to the context. Adapting trainable sparsity to video understanding is practically relevant.
Evaluation covers eight benchmarks spanning long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial reasoning, and includes a dense baseline fine-tuned on the same dataset.
There are meaningful accuracy gains, particularly on Tomato and LSDBench. VideoNSA achieves competitive performance across the evaluated domains and operates at 128K context despite training at 36K.

The appendix provides substantial empirical analysis, including static-gate ablations, context and attention-budget sweeps, kernel comparisons, and a reported training-cost reduction from 5280 to 4600 H100 GPU hours.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited relative to NSA: compression, block selection, sliding-window attention, and learned branch gates are inherited. The contribution primarily consists of modality-specific application, frame-aligned pooling, and fine-tuning. Experiments do not isolate these video-specific choices against a straightforward NSA adaptation.

The central efficiency claims are overstated. Figure 26 shows approximately equal latency to FlashAttention at 128K and worse latency at shorter contexts; several sparse baselines are faster at 128K. Its roughly 3.1× speedup is relative to the separate full-attention implementation, not FlashAttention. End-to-end inference and peak-memory measurements are missing.

The advertised 3.6% attention budget omits the compression branch and dense text attention. Attending from each video query to O(L/s) compressed blocks retains an O(L²/s) term for fixed block size, contradicting the suggested linear complexity of that branch. Table 35 reports practical FLOPs at 56% of FlashAttention, underscoring the difference between the advertised budget and actual computation.

Accuracy improvements over strong sparse baselines are often small: Table 1 improves LongVideoBench by 0.5 points and TimeScope by 0.6, ties MInference on LongTimeScope, and trails XAttention on VSIBench. No uncertainty estimates establish the reliability of these differences. Comparisons also lack matched accuracy–latency tradeoffs and similarly fine-tuned sparse alternatives.

The ablations do not specify whether reduced-branch variants were independently trained or merely disabled at inference. Consequently, their large performance drops do not establish architectural necessity. Replacing learned gates with averages likewise measures sensitivity to an inference intervention rather than conclusively demonstrating superiority over trained static gates.

Scaling claims and reported results are inconsistent. Table 27 shows degradation from 64K to 128K on MLVU, LongTimeScope, and VSIBench, contrary to claims of consistently improving performance. Tables 1 and 3 report different VideoNSA scores without explaining the settings. These discrepancies weaken confidence in the evaluation protocol.

The attention-sink analysis is descriptive rather than causal. Pooling, independently normalized branches, and sigmoid gating complicate comparisons with dense attention, yet a common threshold is used without establishing comparable normalization. No intervention demonstrates that reducing the measured sinks causes the accuracy gains.
